title: Facts, stats and trivia ahead of the 2026 Qatar GP
excerpt:
The closing triple header of the 2026 Formula 1 season continues this weekend as the Lusail International Circuit hosts Round 22 on the calendar, the Qatar Grand Prix.

Free Practice 1 and 2 will take place on Friday, November 27, followed by Free Practice 3 and Qualifying on Saturday, November 28, and the Grand Prix itself on Sunday, November 29.

Vital statistics

First Grand Prix – 2021

Track Length – 5.419km

Lap record – 1m 22.384s, Lando Norris, McLaren, 2024

Most pole positions – Max Verstappen (2)

Most wins – Max Verstappen (3)

Trivia – 2021 represented the first time Qatar had ever hosted an F1 race

Pole run to Turn 1 braking point – 403 metres

Overtakes completed in 2025 – 41

Safety Car probability – 75%*

Virtual Safety Car probability – 50%*

Pit stop time loss – 26.17 seconds

*From the previous four races in Qatar

The driver’s verdict

Jolyon Palmer, former Renault F1 driver: Qatar is full of medium-speed corners and flowing sections. Given that it’s not a huge braking circuit, it’s just about finding the optimum downforce level for the car.

There’s one good overtaking opportunity, and that comes down the lengthy start/finish straight.

The kerbs can be quite punishing, so drivers will need to be careful there, but conversely, as it’s a night race, that will help the tyres a little bit compared to the afternoon heat.

Everything to know about the Lusail International Circuit

Qatar GP polesitters

2025 – Oscar Piastri (McLaren)

2024 – George Russell (Mercedes)*

2023 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2021 – Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

*Max Verstappen set the fastest time in Qualifying but was demoted one place due to a penalty

Qatar GP winners

2025 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2024 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2023 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2021 – Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

Tyre and strategy insight

“For this race, Pirelli has selected the three hardest compounds in its range: the C1 as hard, the C2 as medium, and the C3 as soft,” reads Pirelli’s weekend preview. “The choice is dictated by the characteristics of the Qatari circuit, which generates a particularly high level of wear, especially on the front-left tyre.

“The circuit features 16 corners and its high level of severity stems from the succession of high-speed turns, which subject the tyres to continuous stress for much of the lap. The relatively smooth track surface and the high track temperatures can encourage graining on all compounds, a phenomenon that further increases wear.

“Despite operating in very demanding conditions, the tyres deliver consistent performance throughout the stint. Experience from previous years has shown that performance degradation remains relatively limited even when wear levels are high.

“To prevent tyres from being used beyond their intended life, managing degradation while placing excessive fatigue on the structure, Pirelli has introduced, in agreement with the FIA, a maximum stint length of 27 laps for each set. As a result, the race will inevitably be a minimum two-stop event for all drivers.

“The maximum lap limit has been increased compared to last year because the 2026 tyres feature a further reinforced construction and the cars generate lower levels of aerodynamic load than their 2025 predecessors.

“The introduction of this restriction, as an alternative to other measures such as increasing minimum starting pressures, will allow drivers to push harder during their stints, reducing the need for pace management.”

Current form

Max Verstappen arrives into the weekend off the back of winning a frenetic Las Vegas Grand Prix, with the result meaning that the Red Bull driver now has an even stronger hold on second place in the drivers’ standings behind the already-crowned World Champion Kimi Antonelli.

Having scored nine consecutive podium finishes during the second half of the season, Verstappen remains one of the favourites in Qatar – particularly given that the Dutchman has triumphed across F1’s last three visits to the Lusail International Circuit.

McLaren have also experienced success at the circuit – with Oscar Piastri taking his first win of any kind during the Sprint in 2023 (see below for this iconic moment) as well as claiming pole position last year – and the squad will be keen to carry some momentum into this weekend after earning a double podium finish in Las Vegas.

Over at Mercedes, the Silver Arrows will be hoping for a better outcome after missing out on a potential win last time out, with Antonelli experiencing an issue on the last lap that dropped him back to P4 while George Russell hit the barriers when trying to overtake Antonelli, leaving him down in ninth.

The Briton also saw his rivalry with Verstappen reignited during the weekend, with both making comments about one another following an incident between them in free practice. Will the dispute have an impact on how the pair go racing in Qatar?

Elsewhere, Ferrari were faced with a difficult situation after contact occurred when Charles Leclerc tried to make a move on Lewis Hamilton, an incident that Leclerc received a 10-second time penalty for. With Team Principal Fred Vasseur stating that the team would “discuss what happened internally” in the days after, it will be interesting to see the approach that the Scuderia take this weekend.

In the midfield battle, meanwhile, Alpine secured a solid haul of points in Las Vegas while Racing Bulls left with none – but the Enstone-based outfit may still struggle to catch up in the fight for P6, given that the gap stands at 27 points. Audi, on the other hand, are only three points away from seventh-placed Haas, meaning that a good outing for the former could see them move up.

Iconic moment

Qatar played host to the Sprint when it made its return to the calendar in 2023 following a one-year hiatus, and the star of the 100km dash was undoubtedly Oscar Piastri, the Australian having taken pole position for the event before making a strong start off the line.

While he faced pressure from George Russell at the restart following a Safety Car period – allowing the Mercedes to ultimately take the lead – Piastri was the one to benefit from a later Safety Car deployment as he surged back into P1 when the action resumed.

From there the McLaren man kept his cool in humid conditions to claim his first victory of any kind in Formula 1.

title: Everything you need to know about the Lusail International Circuit
excerpt:
The teams and drivers embark on the penultimate round of the 2026 season this weekend, with Qatar playing host to another night race. But how much do you know about the Lusail International Circuit? F1.com has your all-in-one guide…

Key Lusail International Circuit statistics

Circuit length: 5.419km

Number of turns: 16

Number of laps: 57

Race distance: 308.611km

Lap record: 1m 22.384s – Lando Norris (2024)

When was Qatar’s first Grand Prix?

The Lusail International Circuit had already garnered a reputation as a spectacle in MotoGP before it was added to the F1 calendar in 2021, making its debut as part of a Middle Eastern triple header to close the season.

As touched on, it was primarily designed for motorcycle racing, but has proven itself as an exhilarating venue for four-wheel action too.

The warm desert temperatures, high speeds and flowing layout create a unique challenge for both drivers and Pirelli’s tyres, with a 27-lap limit in place across every compound for the 2026 event.

What’s the circuit like to drive?

Drivers will have to move on from the cold weather they got used to last time out in Las Vegas and instead prepare for soaring temperatures in the cockpit, despite the on-track sessions taking place around and after sunset.

While there are minimal elevation changes, the high G-forces and relentless direction changes add to the conditions, making the circuit especially demanding.

Jolyon Palmer, former Renault F1 driver, explained: “Qatar is full of medium-speed corners and flowing sections.

“Given that it’s not a huge braking circuit, it’s just about finding the optimum downforce level for the car.

“There’s one good overtaking opportunity, and that comes down the lengthy start/finish straight.

“The kerbs can be quite punishing, so drivers will need to be careful there, but conversely, as it’s a night race, that will help the tyres a little bit compared to the afternoon heat.”

It’s just about finding the optimum downforce level for the car.Jolyon Palmer, former F1 driver

Where are the Straight Mode zones and overtake detection?

As a reminder, and as explained in our pre-season summary of regulation changes, Straight Mode is a different aerodynamic configuration that allows cars to reduce their drag, making them more efficient when accelerating up towards top speed.

The rear wing continues to open up a gap – just like it did when drivers used DRS (the Drag Reduction System) in the past – but now the front wing also moves. The uppermost front wing elements drop down at the same time the rear wing’s top element does.

This is a mode that is used on every single lap in dry conditions, in every area that is designated for it. Essentially, the car will adapt between two different configurations depending on where it is on the track, providing maximum downforce in corners but then less drag on straights.

In Qatar, there are four designated Straight Mode zones, commencing with a run along the start/finish straight, then between Turns 3 and 4, between Turns 10 and 12, and a final one from Turn 15 to 16.

Meanwhile, Overtake Mode replaces DRS and is a new power mode that allows a driver to recharge more electrical energy, and generate an additional electrical power profile, so they can sustain a higher speed for a longer period.

There is one detection point per lap for this mode – expected to be out of the final corner on many occasions, leading onto a long straight – and it will be available to drivers on the following lap as long as they stay within a second of the car in front at that detection point.

Around the Lusail International Circuit, the Overtake Detection point comes as drivers exit Turn 16, while the Overtake Activation line follows at the beginning of the start/finish straight.

Five fun facts about the Qatar Grand Prix

Max Verstappen has won three of the four Qatar Grands Prix that have taken place (the race didn’t feature in 2022), with Lewis Hamilton the only other driver to have triumphed in the standard format

McLaren’s Oscar Piastri claimed his first victory of any kind in the Sprint at the Lusail International Circuit back in 2023

Unlike Red Bull, Mercedes and McLaren, Ferrari have never led a lap in Qatar

The circuit was built in just over a year and hosted its inaugural MotoGP round in 2004

Over 1km of the track’s total length is made up of the main straight, which provides plenty of overtaking opportunities into Turn 1

title: 2027 line-ups confirmed: Who is on the grid for next season?
excerpt:
With Ollie Bearman now confirmed at Haas for next season, the 2027 grid is finally complete. So, which teams have changed their line-ups, who is sticking with their current pairings and how many new faces are on the grid next season? Read on to find out…

Mercedes: Kimi Antonelli and George Russell

Mercedes are set for their third season running Kimi Antonelli and George Russell together, but while the drivers are the same, the dynamic might be entirely different. Antonelli is no longer the young, rookie teenager who made so many mistakes at the start of his F1 career.

Instead, he will go into 2027 as a World Champion, a proven race winner and someone who knows he can perform under the highest of pressures. Russell’s job is to step up from a disappointing 2026 campaign and match his team mate week in, week out.

Their car is unlikely to start next season with the same pace advantage that they enjoyed in the first half of 2026, so both drivers know they are in for a battle with Red Bull, Ferrari and McLaren if they want to retain the Teams’ title next year for Mercedes.

Team Principal: Toto Wolff

Wolff remains in charge at Mercedes, having overseen the team since 2013. He was at the helm for their success at the start of the turbo-hybrid era where he guided them to those eight straight Teams’ titles from 2014 to 2021.

And now he has helped them get back to the top, winning both titles in 2026, the Constructors’ sealed in Sao Paulo with three rounds to go. But whether they can stay out front remains to be seen.

Ferrari: Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc

Ferrari are sticking with Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc for 2027, despite several on-track moments between the pair across the 2026 season. Hamilton will be entering his third season with the Scuderia, having won a Grand Prix with the team for the first time this year back in Barcelona.

He also took his first Grand Prix pole in red in 2026, which was a much more successful season than his debut campaign with the team. As for Leclerc, he won back in Silverstone but faced a much bigger challenge from his team mate than he did in 2025.

That challenge has led to the two sharing the same piece of track multiple times in 2026, with flash points in Mexico City and Las Vegas. With no designated ‘number one’ driver, Ferrari will have their hands full keeping both marquee names happy heading into the new year.

Team Principal: Fred Vasseur

Vasseur remains at the helm of Ferrari for the fifth straight season, despite rumours midway through 2026 that linked Christian Horner with the team. Ferrari spent much of the early part of the year as Mercedes’ closest rivals, before encountering some patchy form late on.

By far the biggest issue for Vasseur to contend with is keeping both his drivers happy, with the Team Principal having no issues publicly blaming Leclerc for the intra-team crash in Las Vegas. But he also needs to oversee the car direction in the off-season, with Ferrari out-developed by the likes of Red Bull in 2026.

Red Bull: Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar

Hadjar stepped up to the Red Bull team from Racing Bulls for 2026 and by and large, has impressed. As such, the team have retained his services for 2027 where he will once again partner Verstappen.

The Dutchman is finishing 2026 much stronger than he started it, the RB22 undergoing one of the biggest development arcs in the field. After a dismal first three races in 2026, Verstappen has won four of the last six – starting in Malaysia – with Red Bull looking well set to challenge the might of Mercedes next year.

Verstappen signed a long-term contract back in August that keeps him at the team until 2030, showing his commitment to the Red Bull family. And with an unchanged line up, Red Bull will be hoping the continuity will aid their chances of a championship-charge next year.

Team Principal: Laurent Mekies

Mekies remains at the helm of Red Bull after navigating his first full season in charge. It was not an easy year to steer either, with the car starting the season reasonably uncompetitively. And with an all-new engine too – courtesy of Red Bull Ford Powertrains – there was certainly plenty to keep Mekies busy in 2026.

He also did well to secure Verstappen’s services at a time where Red Bull were not impressing on track, and there seemed to be some disquiet in the Dutchman’s camp. But whether he can deliver titles to the team in 2027 remains to be seen.

McLaren: Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri

It is more of the same for McLaren, who have 2025 World Champion Norris driving for them alongside Piastri. The team have endured an up and down 2026 campaign, ceding control of both championships to Mercedes.

Their year could not have started worse, with two DNS results for Piastri in the first two races, while Norris also failed to make the start line in China. But the car improved, and Norris even delivered wins in 2026 – something that looked highly unlikely at the start of the year.

Norris is far and away the most experienced McLaren driver in history now, and seems to have established himself as half a step ahead of Piastri, whose 2026 season has not gone to plan, after a 2025 when he came so close to claiming the title himself.

Whether the Australian can step up in 2027 remains to be seen, but the team have plenty of work to do over the winter to further understand the regulations and exploit the potential of that Mercedes power unit.

Team Principal: Andrea Stella

Stella remains in charge of McLaren, having led the team since the end of 2022. He retains Zak Brown’s confidence, the American CEO celebrating ten years with McLaren himself at the recent Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Stella and Brown have overseen McLaren’s rise from the back of the field to World Champions, and while they no longer set the pace at the front of the field, the team have the experience within the ranks to unlock these new regulations.

Stella has also made sure McLaren don’t stay still, by recruiting the likes of Red Bull’s Gianpiero Lambiase to add even more experience to the team.

Racing Bulls: Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad

Racing Bulls had a new driver line up in 2026, with rookie Lindblad joining Lawson at the team. Those two excelled across the year, taking Racing Bulls to multiple double points finishes as the team climbed to an unprecedented P5 in the Championship.

Lawson was drafted up to Red Bull for three races midway through the season following Hadjar’s injury, with Yuki Tsunoda stepping in. Lindblad did an exceptional job to lead the team and help Tsunoda get up to speed, impressing with his maturity in his debut season despite being just 19-years-old.

There was some late will-they-won’t-they drama as the team assessed whether their drivers had done enough to stay on, with the talented Nikola Tsolov waiting in the wings, but in the end Racing Bulls opted for experience and retained Lawson and Lindblad.

Team Principal: Alan Permane

Permane’s first full season in charge of Racing Bulls has gone well, with the team impressing on the track and regularly scoring points. They seem to have worked out how to get the best from their Red Bull Ford Powertrains engine, and have designed a car that behaves as expected.

Whether they can maintain that form into 2027 will be the next test, with the midfield set to be every bit as closely matched next season as the fight up front. F1 veteran Permane will also be under pressure to assess his drivers and find the next superstar, with Tsolov unlikely to remain on the bench indefinitely.

Alpine: Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto

Alpine confirmed Gasly first in 2026, and then took a little bit more time to follow suit with Colapinto. But the team has opted to stick with the same line-up for next year, with the Argentine racer entering his fourth season but only his second full campaign.

As for Gasly, he has been with Alpine since 2023 and seems content to stay with the Anglo-French team. They have enjoyed some success together, and 2026 yielded far more positive results that the previous season.

The highlight was Monza, where Gasly secured pole for the team on merit in dry conditions. But there have been tough times as well for Alpine, with Colapinto taking his team mate out in Baku – a result that did not help the team’s quest for fifth in the Constructors’.

Team Principal: Flavio Briatore / Steve Nielsen

Alpine operate a structure with Flavio Briatore as Executive Adviser and Steve Nielsen as Managing Director. The structure seems to be working for the team, who jumped from last in the standings in 2025 to sixth in 2026.

Haas: Ollie Bearman and Esteban Ocon

Haas are the only team fielding a different driver line up for 2027. They started this season with Bearman partnered by Esteban Ocon, but parted ways with the Frenchman in Mexico. Reserve Driver Ryo Hirakawa then raced once for the team, before Rafael Camara was brought in for the final four races.

The F2 star had already been signed for the 2027 season, so the rookie has got a little headstart in terms of gaining Formula 1 experience. His debut race was on home soil in Brazil, and with that weekend featuring plenty of treacherous wet conditions, it proved a baptism of fire for the 21-year-old.

He at least has Bearman to lean on next year, the British driver entering his third full season with the team. He will be expected to step up as the experienced member of the pairing, but will be hoping for a more competitive car after this season’s VF-26 did not perform as well as expected.

Team Principal: Ayao Komatsu

Komatsu remains in charge of Haas, a role he has enjoyed since replacing Guenther Steiner in 2024. This year saw plenty of challenges, from a car that was not always fast, upgrades that did not work as planned and some late season driver line up changes.

Through it all Komatsu has steadied the ship, but he knows on track performance counts for everything in the fast-paced world of F1.

Audi: Nico Hulkenberg and Gabriel Bortoleto

Audi have also opted to stick with their existing driver line up, pairing the experience of Hulkenberg with the youth of Bortoleto. Those two are into their third year together, and seem to get on well.

Their 2026 campaign was their first with an Audi engine in the car, which caused some early hiccups with reliability. But midway through the season, their upgrade packages started to pay dividends as the team went on a run of five top 10 finishes in six races.

Bortoleto more than proved he is the real deal, regularly beating his team mate over both one lap and in the races. There was no huge highlight like last year’s Silverstone podium for Hulkenberg, but the team now have a very solid platform to build from in 2027.

Team Principal: Mattia Binotto / Allan McNish

Much like Alpine, Audi have adopted a slightly different management structure following the early season departure of Team Principal Jonathan Wheatley. Allan McNish has assumed many of those responsibilities under the title of Racing Director, while Mattia Binotto still oversees the team as Head of Audi F1.

Williams: Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon

Williams have retained the same driver line up in Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon for another season, in the hope that those two can spearhead a recovery up the order.

After a strong 2025 season, 2026 has been disappointing for the Grove-based team who have fallen short on competitiveness. The car took the blame, leaving Sainz and Albon suffering early exits in Qualifying and races fighting down the back of the field.

There have been a few moments of joy – Sainz’s recent drive to P8 on merit in Las Vegas one such example. But with one proven race-winner in their ranks in the Spaniard, plus Albon who has also competed right at the front of the field, Williams need to deliver a better car, lest those two start to debate their future options.

Team Principal: James Vowles

Vowles oversaw Williams’ revival in 2025, but this season the team have fallen short of expectations. Having long signalled 2026 as the aim for the team to return towards the front of the grid, with the new regulations offering a chance to shake up the pecking order, instead Williams started the year late, with an overweight car.

As such, Vowles might find himself under some pressure in 2027, unless the team can start the season much more strongly and deliver a car that is capable of fighting for points.

Aston Martin: Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll

Alonso’s future looked uncertain for parts of 2026, but he has committed to the team for at least one more year. That means he will be embarking on his 24th season in the sport. Partnering Stroll once again, both drivers will be hoping for a much more competitive car and engine next year.

Neither has much to show for this season, after struggles with both the chassis and the Honda power unit. Reliability needs to improve in 2027 if the team wish to keep Alonso happy, although they are letting him compete in the Dakar Rally in January, which should get his competitive juices flowing.

Team Principal: Adrian Newey

Newey has not attended many races in 2026, instead spending much of his time back at HQ trying to sort out what went wrong with the AMR26, and working out how to fix the issues for 2027.

Instead, Chief Trackside Officer Mike Krack has run the team on many race weekends, and faced the media after a string of disappointing results that at the time of writing, have yielded just three top 10 finishes.

Cadillac: Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas

Cadillac are the first completely new entry into F1 for a decade, but they have not found their debut season easy. Opting for the experience of Perez and Bottas seemed wise, and those two have managed to deliver plenty of feedback across the year.

The team were reportedly contemplating whether to keep the Finn for 2027, but have decided that the experience Bottas brings counts for a lot, despite the former Mercedes race winner often being slower than Perez on track.

Bottas has also had the worst of the reliability luck, failing to either start or finish 11 times in the first 21 races, compared to Perez who has recorded five DNF results in the same timespan.

Team Principal: Marcin Budkowski

Cadillac began the year with Graeme Lowdon in charge, but after a string of reliability issues mainly to do with overheating brakes, they opted to replace Lowdon with Budkowski in the summer break.

Budkowski has a wealth of F1 experience, having been at Renault and Alpine between 2017 and 2022. He has also worked at McLaren and Ferrari, and spent three years with the FIA in their technical department.

His job is simple – make Cadillac more competitive, so they can fight for points with the rest of the midfield sooner rather than later.

title: Why Bearman’s new Haas deal took so long to get over the line
excerpt:
Ollie Bearman's Formula 1 future is officially secure after Haas announced he'll be in the car for at least 2027. But what took so long?

As worst kept secrets in the F1 paddock go, Bearman continuing with Haas for 2027 is right up there.

Haas have long made clear that they wanted to keep him after he levelled up in his second season with them in 2026, outshining team mate and one-time race winner Esteban Ocon.

Of Haas' 31 points, Bearman has scored 23 of them and it has been his improved consistency, the way he motivates the team around him and the overall quality of his feedback that has really impressed. In their eyes, he's a top-line driver.

But it wasn't Haas' decision alone as to whether or not they could keep him as Bearman is part of their engine supplier Ferrari's junior programme, and they need their agreement.

Sources say Ferrari are very happy with Bearman's progress at Haas and continue to rate him highly, having invested in him since they added the Briton to their academy in 2021.

They want to keep him within the Ferrari family not just to get the return on their investment but because they believe he's talented enough to step up to the factory team at some point in the future.

Right now, though, they have no space. They tied up Charles Leclerc on a new deal earlier this year, which runs beyond 2028, and while Lewis Hamilton is only signed up until the end of 2027, he's hinted he's keen to stay.

However, there is clearly tension inside the team right now with Leclerc and Hamilton tangling again last time out in Las Vegas. And that highlights why Ferrari want someone of Bearman's quality on their books should they require someone to step up.

It's a tricky scenario for Bearman, though. He is eternally grateful to Ferrari for giving him the chance, first with a place on their academy and then as a super sub in Saudi Arabia in 2024 which really put him on the map.

And it's clear his dream is to race in red and be a factory race driver. But he's also aware that time waits for no one and he can't wait around forever.

If Hamilton signs up with Ferrari beyond the end of 2027, Bearman is facing at least two more years with Haas (taking him to four overall).

At the same time, he's going up against Rafa Camara, who joined the Ferrari junior programme at the same time as him, at Haas – and that gives Ferrari a proper comparison of their juniors.

Bearman to continue with Haas for 2027

With all that in mind, it makes complete sense for Bearman's management team to want to make sure they get the right contract.

It should be noted that this was the first big negotiation for Bearman and his management in F1, given the first deals were no-brainers for them as they got them into Ferrari and then onto the grid. It's understandable that it has taken a little time.

Sources say that it was never really about the money but rather agreeing on options and exit clauses that suit all parties.

An agreement was reached ahead of this weekend's Qatar Grand Prix, which will see Bearman race for Haas next year and what is believed to be 2028 as well, depending on, as I understand it, a certain set of circumstances including the state of play at Ferrari.

In this way, everyone wins:

Ferrari have someone they rate on the grid driving for a team that brings the best out of Bearman and helps drive his development. They also have access to him if they need him in the future.

Bearman has security for Haas for a couple of years. He remains on the pathway for Ferrari but has options to do something different if there's no room at the inn for the foreseeable future.

Haas get a driver who is delivering massively for them for a couple of years and who will be a good benchmark for their new rookie Camara.

And if they want to change tack at the end of next year or beyond, they can all sit down and discuss it in good faith given there is a good relationship between all stakeholders.

For now, Bearman and Haas can focus on ending this season strongly and delivering a strong campaign next year.

title: Bearman to continue with Haas for 2027
excerpt:
The Haas Formula 1 team have confirmed that Ollie Bearman has re-signed with the American outfit.

The Briton becomes the final driver to be confirmed for the 2027 season, with Bearman set to remain at the team for a third consecutive campaign.

The announcement was made on Thursday ahead of the Qatar Grand Prix after speculation surrounding Bearman's future with the team had grown in recent weeks.

Ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix last weekend, Bearman had expressed his disappointment at the delay in finalising the deal.

But speaking after the announcement, Team Principal Ayao Komatsu said: “Continuing with Ollie into 2027 was a natural decision for us.

“We’ve seen his growth, his commitment, and the quality he brings to the team, both on and off the track. He has a tremendous work ethic and a strong desire to develop both himself and the team, and there is no better person, in my opinion, to lead this team forward. TGR Haas F1 Team has one of the most exciting driver pairings on the grid, and I look forward to seeing Ollie flourish further with this incredible team.”

“It’s no secret that I’m delighted to be continuing with TGR Haas F1 Team into 2027,” said Bearman. “This team has played an integral role in my development, and I’ve felt a huge amount of belief and support from everyone here.

“We’ve got big ambitions to keep pushing forward, and I’m excited to lead that work, building on what we’ve achieved, and striving for even more together – we have unfinished business.”

Bearman, who is a Ferrari junior driver, made his F1 debut with the Scuderia as a stand-in for Carlos Sainz at the 2024 Saudi Arabian Grand Prix, becoming the team's youngest-ever driver in the process.

He raced for Haas in two further Grands Prix that season before becoming a full-time driver in 2025, taking a best result of P4 in Mexico City, and this season currently sits P13 in the Drivers' standings.

He will be joined at Haas next season by fellow Ferrari junior, Rafael Camara, who was moved into the second seat at Haas early after the team parted ways with Esteban Ocon.

The Brazilian is also set to contest the final two rounds of the year after it was confirmed he would not finish his F2 campaign despite leading the standings.

title: FIA confirm Williams’ minor overspend breach of 2025 Cost Cap
excerpt:
Formula 1's governing body the FIA have completed their review of the F1 teams’ and power unit manufacturers’ compliance with the 2025 Financial Regulations, with Williams found to have committed an unintentional minor overspend breach and a procedural breach, while Alpine also made a procedural breach.

As part of the review by the Cost Cap Administration (CCA) – a process that took eight months – all 11 Formula 1 teams and all five power unit (PU) manufacturers submitted financial documentation from 2025.

Nine of the 11 teams and all five power unit manufacturers were found in compliance for 2025, but Williams were found to have unintentionally committed a minor overspend breach and a procedural breach.

In a document confirming that an Accepted Breach Agreement (ABA) has been entered into between Williams and the Cost Cap Administration, it was explained that “there is no evidence that WGPE [Williams Grand Prix Engineering] gained or sought to gain any advantage (sporting or otherwise) from the identified breaches”, and that “the minor overspend breach amounts to £627k and therefore, with 0.48% over the 2025 Cost Cap, falls at the lower end of the <5% minor overspend range”.

Williams will subsequently pay a financial penalty for the breach, as well as taking a 1.5% reduction in wind tunnel and CFD testing over the next 12 months.

The team said in a statement: “The breach relates to administrative costs we incurred making changes to our company structure. We believed these costs fell outside of the cap. Following discussions with the FIA, we have agreed to resolve the matter in line with their interpretation that the costs should have been in cap.

“The FIA has noted that Williams did not gain any sporting or financial advantage, and nor did we ever seek to. It has also noted that we acted cooperatively and in good faith throughout the review process.

“Integrity is central to what Williams stands for and we can now close this case and remain focused on our future. We have always been and will continue to be strong supporters of the Cost Cap, which naturally requires accurate policing to be effective.”

A procedural breach was identified for Alpine, with the FIA confirming that “there is no evidence that Alpine gained or sought to gain any advantage from the inaccurate exclusions or adjustments of certain costs; and notwithstanding the Cost Cap Administration’s determination of procedural breach, Alpine’s relevant costs in respect of the 2025 Reporting Period were below the 2025 Cost Cap”.

An Accepted Breach Agreement has been entered into between the team and the Cost Cap Administration, with Alpine set to pay a financial penalty and bear the costs incurred by the Cost Cap Administration in connection with its investigation of the Procedural Breach and the preparation of the ABA.

title: 5 storylines we're excited about ahead of the Qatar GP
excerpt:
Fresh from one of the most exciting races in recent memory, it’s time to shift focus to the Gulf for the final two rounds of the 2026 season. There wasn’t only great racing to talk about after Las Vegas, but frustrations and controversies among teams and drivers that could still be simmering under the surface as we make the trip to Qatar.

Verstappen and Russell’s rift

Tensions rose in Las Vegas during the final practice session of the weekend, particularly between Max Verstappen and George Russell.

With the first two sessions impacted by rain, and no dry running possible, FP3 was a busy session with drivers looking to get as much data as they could before locking in their set-ups ahead of qualifying. That led to a moment where Russell and Verstappen fought on track, and Russell later spoke out against the Dutchman's approach.

“I’m not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this, and walk around like they’re bigger and better than everyone else,” Russell said. “Somebody has got to stand up to that guy.”

The pair started alongside each other on the front row and delivered a thrilling fight in a remarkable race until Russell hit the barrier trying to overtake team mate Kimi Antonelli, with Verstappen going on to secure his fourth victory in six races.

Following his win, Verstappen was then asked about Russell’s comments and was similarly in no mood to smooth over relations.

“He speaks a lot next to the track,” Verstappen said. “And honestly, for me, it doesn’t really bother me, because he’s so far below my level, it doesn’t make sense for me anyway to try and challenge that. So it doesn’t bother me.

“And, today, karma is a b****. It was honestly fantastic when I looked in my mirror and I saw what was happening [when Russell hit the wall]. I was like, ‘fantastic, my day is only getting better’. And then when I crossed the line in first, my day was complete.”

Qatar was the scene of a disagreement between the two drivers back in 2024, after Verstappen was given a grid penalty for impeding Russell during Qualifying. Verstappen said he “lost all respect” for Russell following the stewards’ hearing, and they now return to the scene of that incident after another verbal joust.

Driver drama at Ferrari

If Russell was frustrated with the way his race panned out in Las Vegas, then so too was his former team mate Lewis Hamilton after an incident-filled Saturday night.

Hamilton was penalised for leaving the track at Turn 7 and gaining an advantage in a fight with Lando Norris in the first half of the race, before then being hit by team mate Charles Leclerc at the same corner later on.

PALMER: Where do Ferrari go from here after Las Vegas clash?

The contact tapped Hamilton into a spin and limited him to seventh place at the flag, with Leclerc earning his own 10-second time penalty for the collision and being demoted to tenth place.

Team Principal Fred Vasseur described the incident as “more than unacceptable” and accused Leclerc of a lack of respect, with the fact he had spoken to both drivers after their battle in Mexico City only adding to Vasseur’s frustration.

The inference was he would take his time before working out his next move, and Thursday will be the first chance to hear from the drivers if there have been any repercussions.

Bearman’s contractual situation at Haas

Following the confirmation in the run-up to the Las Vegas Grand Prix that Liam Lawson, Arvid Lindblad and Valtteri Bottas are all retaining their seats for 2027, only one position remains unconfirmed.

That’s the place of Ollie Bearman at Haas, where at the time of writing a formal announcement has yet to be forthcoming.

Bearman will still race for Haas next season, and confirmation is expected imminently, but the 21-year-old was clearly frustrated when he spoke to the media in Las Vegas, expressing his disappointment and saying there is “no excuse” for his contract to still have been unsigned.

Once there is an official announcement, it will be interesting to see if Bearman can offer any further insight into what was causing the delay, with his future slightly more complex than some drivers as it involves both Ferrari and Haas at this stage.

Komatsu insists there is 'no doubt' over Bearman's Haas seat

Camara forgoes F2 title bid

While Bearman was still waiting to be able to confirm his future, his team mate received certainty over his own plans.

Rafael Camara made his Haas debut at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix and retained his seat in Las Vegas, as the team decided how to move forward following the sidelining of Esteban Ocon. While Camara was only announced for Las Vegas in the build-up to that race, the lack of news regarding the remaining two rounds suggested there was an outside chance he could still return to Formula 2 to try and defend his championship lead.

That notion has now been put to bed, with Camara confirmed in the Haas for the remainder of this season, ahead of his full-time drive in 2027.

F2 regulations state a driver cannot also compete in F1 in the same weekend, so Camara will now be unable to add to his points tally in the feeder series, and is likely to see one of Nikola Tsolov or Alex Dunne take the championship ahead of him.

A high speed test and minimum two-stop

The Lusail International Circuit could not be much different from the Las Vegas Strip Circuit when it comes to track characteristics. Aside from being a night race, the two share few similarities.

A much warmer climate awaits this weekend, but the drivers will also be having to work hard through the numerous high speed corners that push a car to the limits of its aerodynamic performance. The track surface is also extremely rough compared to Las Vegas, and there are some punishing kerbs if you run over them on too many occasions.

Last year, Pirelli imposed a maximum lap count of 25 laps per tyre set in Qatar, due to the energy loads, thermal stress and tread wear that the track creates. This time around, that limit has been increased to 27 laps per set, but with a 57-lap race it means it will still be impossible to complete the distance without changing tyres on two occasions.

Laps in every session count and the total is cumulative, but the reconnaissance laps to the grid and formation lap will not be included in the total, nor will any laps after the chequered flag.

title: Jack Whitehall on why Antonelli surprised him in first meeting
excerpt:
Jack Whitehall has shared the story of how Kimi Antonelli took him by surprise when they first met, with the actor and comedian insisting that the new World Champion is “not like any sportsman I’ve ever interacted with”.

After hosting F1-75 Live at the start of the 2025 season, Whitehall has since become an official Friend of F1 and even participated in the recent LEGO race held at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

The Briton has also collaborated with Mercedes as part of a series for the team’s partner Marriott Bonvoy, meaning that he has been able to spend time with Antonelli and George Russell – and says he found himself surprised by Antonelli’s nature outside of the car.

“Because I’ve done over the last year a lot of work with Mercedes and I’ve been around them a lot, I have grown very fond of George and Kimi, and so it’s been really nice to be around them as they’ve had this kind of upturn in form,” Whitehall explained on the latest episode of official podcast F1 Beyond The Grid.

“Particularly with Kimi, watching him have this incredible season and being a little bit adjacent to it at times has been so amazing. He’s not like any sportsman that I’ve ever interacted with.

“I’ve done lots of stuff with footballers and rugby players, and there’s always an element of, I don’t know, ego and charisma. Not that Kimi doesn’t have charisma, but he’s just so unassuming and humble, and sweet and impish, and it’s insane.

“Something must just switch the minute he gets behind the wheel in that car and he just turns into an absolute beast.”

When asked if Antonelli is always pulling pranks – given that the Italian has become known for his fondness of a practical joke – Whitehall recounted the amusing story of when he first met the 20-year-old.

“He’s so silly and mischievous,” said Whitehall. “The first time I ever met with him, we were doing a little sketch in Singapore and we were filming in a hotel room.

“Everyone was kind of worried, and again this always happens when you’re filming with a sportsman – they’re all worried about whether they’re going to be in a good mood when they come in, and how long they’re going to have with you to do the little bit because they’ve got this insane schedule that they have to keep to.

“He came in, he walks in, he’s friendly to everyone, and genuinely all he was asking about was whether he could jump on the bed, because he wanted to jump up and down on the bed!

“And I was like ‘Is he doing a bit here? You’re literally like the Kimi Antonelli persona that I have in my head, and it’s just real’. He was just so unassuming, and he was grinning and fun.”

Whitehall also went on to share his experiences with other well-known names in F1 during the conversation, including Russell, Lewis Hamilton and Toto Wolff.

title: Lando Norris confirms key McLaren meeting topic on shocking error anniversary
excerpt:
Lando Norris has confirmed that McLaren's disastrous 2025 Qatar Grand Prix strategy call will come up in his pre-weekend meeting with the team, a year on since the error derailed his title bid in Lusail.

The Briton finished fourth at last year's race after McLaren opted to leave both him and Oscar Piastri out on track during a lap seven safety car, caused by a clash between Nico Hulkenberg and Pierre Gasly.

If we would have boxed, we still would have been stuck in the pit lane, a lot more people would have come out ahead of us, and it wasn't a guarantee we were getting back past them. title: Honda deny problem with Fernando Alonso engine after mysterious issue
excerpt:
Honda and Fernando Alonso have provided contradictory accounts of his perceived power unit issue that saw him pull into the pits to retire at the end of the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Honda has been unable to identify any problems with the power unit in Fernando Alonso's Aston Martin after he retired from the Las Vegas Grand Prix at the final corner.

Alonso pulled into the pit lane at the end of the 50-lap race in Sin City instead of taking the chequered flag, bemoaning an issue with his engine.

However, in the days since, the Japanese marque has still not been able to detect anything wrong with the unit, as it stated shortly after the race.

"We have checked all the data we have now, and during maintenance, we also checked the engine physically," said Shintaro Orihara, Honda's trackside general manager and chief engineer, to media, including RacingNews365.

"At this moment, we haven't found any issues with the engine from the data or from the maintenance. But we will check on Friday how the engine works on this track."

Alonso, who is missing media day at the Qatar Grand Prix as he recovers from a viral infection, is due to be back in his AMR26 for FP2 at the Lusail International Circuit, with Jak Crawford deputising in FP1.

Despite their accounts being at odds, Orihara was keen to express how much Honda "respect" the feedback provided by Alonso.

"We carefully analysed his comments, and we also respect his comments. That's why we checked all the data, and we also checked the engine condition," he said.

"But from the data, at the moment we haven't seen any issues. But as I mentioned, we should check again on Friday to get some feedback from Fernando."

[Article continues below]

Driver

What might be causing the disparity in accounts?

The Las Vegas Strip Circuit is an outlier on the F1 calendar and, due to the energy-poor, high-speed nature of the track, it is not a happy hunting ground for the underpowered Honda engine.

That paucity was exacerbated by the slipstream-fest that was experienced in Nevada, amplifying the shortcomings of the power unit.

"In Las Vegas, it's difficult to analyse how engine performance affects car speed; there is a lot of the tow effect, and also different energy management across two cars," Orihara added. "So our metrics say power itself is okay, but probably we should check carefully on these tracks again...

"Probably, this year, our engine performance is not enough to satisfy or give confidence to the drivers, and then probably they feel the engine performance is not great."

Mike Krack, Aston Martin's chief trackside officer, also defended the situation, stressing caution about jumping to conclusions over the disparity from the information and contradictory accounts from Alonso and Honda.

He detailed how the increased energy usage under the 2026 F1 power unit regulations can make it confusing for a driver to work out what is combustion power and what is from the battery.

"We need to be careful because the K [MGU-K] power is so much higher that as soon as you have even a small variation in K, it could feel like the ICE [internal combustion engine] — and you have different K power in different places," said Krack.

"So very often, for the drivers, it's much more difficult to judge than it used to be in the past. And I think some of it is coming from there."

"There have been many flaws with this power unit, but it's worked quite well at this track because it's made the tows so powerful. So I think, for me, it was pretty cool. I enjoyed it."

title: Ferrari boss sets Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc clear target after latest clash
excerpt:
Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur has called on Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc to bring both cars home with a "solid result" at the Qatar Grand Prix after the latter spun his team-mate in Las Vegas.

The pair were fighting for sixth when Leclerc tried to pass Hamilton up the inside at Turn 7 in Sin City.

The stewards held Leclerc responsible for the collision and gave him a 10-second penalty that dropped him to P10 at the chequered flag. Hamilton recovered to finish seventh despite a 10-second penalty of his own for passing Lando Norris off the track.

Vasseur described Leclerc's mistake as “completely unacceptable” after the race. He said Ferrari had reminded both drivers to think of the team as they raced each other in Las Vegas, having already sat down with them in Brazil to discuss what happened in Mexico City.

The first flashpoint came at Monza in September, when Hamilton took to the gravel at the opening chicane and told Ferrari over the radio that Leclerc had pushed him off. Leclerc later acknowledged he could have given Hamilton more room.

In Mexico City, both Ferraris ran wide at Turn 4 as Leclerc challenged pole-sitter Hamilton for the lead on the opening lap. Leclerc crossed the grass and emerged ahead, earning a five-second penalty, while Max Verstappen passed Hamilton on the exit. Verstappen went on to win by less than a second from Hamilton, with Leclerc fourth.

"We head to Qatar determined to respond as a team and deliver the kind of weekend we expect from ourselves,” Vasseur said.

"Lusail is very different to Las Vegas, with its long sequences of high-speed corners."

Teams will have to factor Friday’s running into their plans for Sunday. The tyre mileage limit applies across the weekend, and each driver will need at least three sets to cover the 57-lap race.

"The 27-lap limit for each set will also make the tyre allocation and strategy management unique for this weekend," the Ferrari boss added.

"We have three practice sessions to prepare the car, and our objective is clear: maximise every part of the weekend to the highest possible standard and bring home a solid result with both cars."

title: Max Verstappen torn into during stunning rebuke: 'That really disgusts me'

Former F1 driver Sebastien Bourdais has accused Max Verstappen of holding his rivals to a standard he does not meet himself, saying the Red Bull driver expects them to go easy on him despite using “every trick in the book” when they race wheel to wheel.

Bourdais, who won four successive Champ Car titles from 2004 to 2007 before joining Toro Rosso, shared how the way Verstappen conducts himself "really bothers" him following the latest flare-up in the long-running tensions between the Dutchman and Mercedes driver George Russell at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

The Frenchman made 27 grand prix starts for Red Bull's sister team across the 2008 and 2009 seasons, but did not hold back when discussing the four-time F1 drivers' champion, saying his claimed double standards appal him.

"I don't like him as a character, because there's something about Max that really bothers me," Bourdais told Eurosport France. "It's the way he always looks at things.

"Basically, he expects the others to race a certain way. When they're racing him, he wants things to play out a certain way. But he thinks he can do whatever he likes. That really disgusts me."

Russell took issue with Verstappen's approach at the Las Vegas Grand Prix after the pair made contact at Turn 14 in final practice. The stewards warned Verstappen for erratic driving after he changed direction under braking.

The Briton told Sky Italia that Verstappen regularly overtook drivers as they prepared to start a flying lap, compromising their runs. "Somebody's got to stand up to that guy," he said.

Verstappen won the race while Russell finished ninth after sliding into the barriers. Asked about Russell's remarks afterwards, Verstappen said the Mercedes driver was "so far below my level" and described seeing his rival go off in his mirrors as "karma", something he laughed at over team radio when he saw the incident in his rearview mirrors.

"At some point you've got to make up your mind," the former Toro Rosso driver added.

title: Toto Wolff issues 'fierce' Mercedes prediction ahead of unique F1 weekend
excerpt:
The Qatar Grand Prix sits as the host of the second-to-last round of the 2026 season.

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff has stated he expects his squad to face "fierce" competition at the front of the field at the Qatar Grand Prix this weekend.

The Brackley-based squad enters the event on the back of a challenging result last time out in Las Vegas.

Both George Russell and Kimi Antonelli were in contention for the win before separate late-race mishaps saw them finish off the podium.

Antonelli ended the race in fourth while Russell had to settle for ninth place after making contact with the barrier.

Wolff insisted the team is primed to get back on track to get over the disappointment of the Las Vegas weekend.

"The best way to move on from a disappointing result is to go racing again," he said.

"Las Vegas didn't end the way we wanted, but we were in the fight at the front all evening and that is something we can take confidence from.

"There was action throughout and plenty of drama. It was a great spectacle for the fans and another reminder of the show F1 can put on."

[Article continues below]

Qatar a 'different challenge'

Qatar hosts the penultimate round of the season this weekend, with the event being the Lusail International Circuit's fifth race since joining the schedule.

It is a race that Red Bull has won three years on the bounce, a streak that Mercedes is looking to end.

"Qatar will be a completely different challenge," Wolff added.

"The Lusail Circuit is relentless: high-speed corners, aggressive kerbs and hot temperatures make it tough on the cars and drivers.

title: Inside the Ferrari meeting that cleared the air – until Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc clashed again
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc reckoned it took "maybe five or 10 minutes" to clear the air with Lewis Hamilton after their first-lap clash in Mexico City — but the next round of evidently-needed discussions may not be as straightforward.

The Ferrari drivers spent the rest of an hour in Fred Vasseur's São Paulo hotel room talking about how to help Ferrari move forward. By the team principal's account, they "left my room joking together".

One race weekend later, at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, Vasseur was on the radio asking Leclerc to come and see him before he spoke to the media.

Fighting for sixth place, Leclerc had tried to pass Hamilton up the inside at Turn 7 in Sin City and tipped his team-mate into a spin. Hamilton recovered to finish seventh. Leclerc crossed the line sixth, but a 10-second penalty dropped him to P10

The first meeting had taken place on the Thursday evening of the Brazilian weekend, four days after the row erupted on the opening lap of the Mexico City Grand Prix.

There, Leclerc had attacked Hamilton around the outside of Turn 4 for the lead, with both cars going off-track. That allowed Max Verstappen to sneak up the inside of Hamilton to run second, with Leclerc ahead.

The Monegasque driver was subsequently handed a five-second time penalty for leaving the track and gaining a lasting advantage, but Hamilton was furious over the radio, declaring that the team had "big problems".

Post-race, he declared that he was "really pi**ed" at losing a straightforward one-two finish, and that Leclerc had a "do or die" attitude when it came to racing him.

Following the talks, both drivers insisted it was case closed. Before the flare-up in Las Vegas, Leclerc offered some further insight into what went on behind closed doors.

"I think everything has been taken out of proportion," Leclerc told media, including RacingNews365. "I’m kind of used to it now, driving for Ferrari for so many years, but things are often taken out of proportion.

"Of course, I mean the goal is not always to agree; that will never happen, and we can have different opinions, and that was the case, for example, in Mexico. We’ve spoken, and we’re completely fine with it.

"It is not that we had to speak for an hour, even though [the meeting] ended up lasting an hour, just because we had a good time and we started speaking about many other things in trying to bring the team together and to help the team go forward.

"But the discussion about the tension was maybe five or 10 minutes, and then the air was clear, and that’s it.

"Fred was definitely involved. He was in the meeting, and he organised the meeting. So we were all three together, and the discussion went very well.

"But as we’ve said, I think very quickly, we only had to speak and after a few sentences, the tension that was there was not there anymore, and it was all fine."

[Article continues below]

Vasseur calls for fresh talks

Even after the collision in Las Vegas, Leclerc stood by his account of the first meeting. "We've had discussions, and I think the discussions have gone very well," he said.

He accepted the stewards' verdict and ultimately took the blame, but said he saw a difference between the two incidents.

In Mexico, he felt both drivers had pushed too hard. In Las Vegas, he believed Hamilton had been watching the McLaren ahead and had not seen him go for the gap.

Hamilton, meanwhile, left it to Ferrari to decide whether the pair needed clearer rules for racing each other, saying that "hopefully in the background they eventually figure it out."

For Vasseur, the instruction had been clear. "I think we had a clear discussion in São Paulo," he said after the race. Ferrari had reminded Leclerc over the radio during the race in Nevada to think about the team while fighting Hamilton.

Leclerc apologised when he saw Vasseur after the flag. The Ferrari boss said he wanted to sit down with both drivers once they had had time to reflect. The outcome of those conversations will become clear on media day in Qatar.

As for what the pair had discussed in that first exchange in Las Vegas, Vasseur put it rather differently from the hour the three had spent together in Brazil, stating: "No, it was not a discussion – I spoke!"

title: Why the Qatar GP is home to a unique and unusual F1 rule
excerpt:
The Qatar Grand Prix will see maximum tyre stints enforced throughout the weekend - but why is the rule in place?

Pirelli will once again enforce a maximum stint limit for the F1 tyres this weekend at the Qatar Grand Prix, which hosts the penultimate round of the season.

It is a move that it has adopted on several occasions in the past during the sport's visit to the Lusail International Circuit.

Maximum tyre stint limits exist as a safety measure, introduced by the FIA and Pirelli to prevent microscopic separation within the tyre carcass from developing into sudden deflation during high-speed running.

At Lusail specifically, the concern has centred on extreme localised front-tyre wear caused by sustained lateral loads and high carcass temperatures through the circuit's continuous fast corners, with Pirelli's evaluations showing that running beyond a set number of laps fully depletes the tread compound's protective layer and exposes the underlying structure to failure risk.

This year, it has increased the maximum permitted tyre stint length for the Qatar Grand Prix to 27 laps, up from 25 last year, with the change rooted in both the tyre construction and this year's cars.

The Italian manufacturer explained that the 2026 tyre range features a further reinforced internal carcass, built to resist fatigue despite being lighter than before.

Pirelli also condensed its dry compound range this year, dropping the softest C6 option to leave five choices from C1 to C5, with the harder end of that range dominating selection at Lusail.

[Article continues below]

Grand Prix

Qatar GP

Pirelli also pointed to the lower aerodynamic load generated by the 2026 generation of cars compared with their 2025 predecessors, reducing the peak cornering stresses that drive carcass wear and localised tread degradation through Lusail's sweeping, high-speed corners.

That drop in load is partly a product of the sport's new technical regulations, which have cut overall downforce by roughly 30 per cent through flatter floors that do away with the full Venturi ground-effect tunnels used between 2022 and 2025.

The cars have also become lighter and more compact, all of which chip away at the mechanical and aerodynamic forces that load up the tyres through Lusail's long, sweeping corners.

The restriction traces back to the 2023 Qatar Grand Prix. That led to an 18-lap stint cap being imposed that weekend.

Concerns over Lusail's demands on tyres stretch back further still, to the inaugural 2021 race, when four drivers suffered sudden front-left punctures amid the sustained lateral loads of the track's high-speed right-handers.

For Sunday's 57-lap race, the 27-lap ceiling still forces at least two pit stops, since two full stints cover only 54 laps. But the extra two laps per stint compared with 2025 widens the strategic window for teams, giving them more freedom to react to a Safety Car or stagger their stops rather than being locked into a rigid split.

With no scope to stretch a set beyond the limit, compound choice is expected to centre on outright pace and degradation resistance across three stints using the harder end of Pirelli's range, rather than any attempt at thermal conservation.

title: Liam Lawson sets 'very strong' Racing Bulls goal after securing F1 future
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has outlined what he wants to achieve with Racing Bulls next season, following confirmation that he will race for the team in F1 next season.

Liam Lawson has set his sights on keeping Racing Bulls at the head of the F1 midfield in 2027 after securing his seat for next season.

He believes the team’s ability to deliver upgrades that work as well on track as they do in the simulator has been central to its push for fifth in the constructors’ championship.

The New Zealander has also been one of the standout performers of 2026. He sits ninth in the drivers’ standings on 89 points, as best of the rest behind the top four teams, 37 clear of his nearest rival, Alpine's Pierre Gasly.

Yet whether Lawson would keep his place on the grid had become one of the main talking points in the driver market, with Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov in contention for his seat.

Racing Bulls ended the speculation on 12 November by retaining Lawson alongside Arvid Lindblad for 2027. Tsolov will serve as reserve driver for both Red Bull teams.

Asked what goals he had set himself for next year, Lawson told media, including RacingNews365: "I think maybe more of the same, really. We want to try and stay on top of the midfield if we can.

"Obviously, we still have some races to go this year, and we want to try and secure that, but to try and keep that momentum into next year and keep the development going."

[Article continues below]

Neither Lawson nor Lindblad scored in the most recent grand prix, in Las Vegas, where Gasly finished fifth and Franco Colapinto sixth to collect 18 points for Alpine, cutting Racing Bulls' advantage from 45 points to 27.

It was the first time since Zandvoort, the first round back after the F1 summer break, that the Faenza-based squad failed to register a point.

With Qatar and Abu Dhabi to come, Racing Bulls leads Alpine by 114 points to 87. Holding on to fifth would give the team its best constructors' championship finish in a history stretching back to its days as Minardi.

"I feel like as a team, everything we've brought to the track this year, the upgrades have worked very, very well," Lawson added.

"It's not that easy sometimes to do that. You sometimes have upgraded simulations that show something that's going to work on a car, and it doesn't always do what you think it's going to do, but for us it has this year.

title: Alpine reveal cause of F1 cost cap breach as FIA sanction issued
excerpt:
Alpine has explained its procedural breach of the FIA cost cap rules for the 2025 F1 season, for which it has received a financial penalty from the motorsport governing body.

The team acknowledged and accepted the findings of the Cost Cap Administration (CAA) in a statement shared with media, including RacingNews365, shortly after the FIA announced its findings.

The Enstone-based squad entered into an Accepted Breach Agreement (ABA) with the FIA on 11 November 2026, which resulted in a fine. However, the amount has not been disclosed.

Alpine was found to have committed "errors and inaccuracies" in its reporting for the 2025 campaign, but as it did not breach the actual cost cap spending limit, it has not been subjected to a sporting punishment, unlike Williams.

The statement from the team spokesperson said: "Alpine Formula One Team acknowledges and accepts the findings of the Cost Cap Administration (CCA) for the 2025 Reporting Period.

"The team accepts that it unknowingly committed a Procedural Breach, which is a result of inaccuracies in the Full Year Reporting Documentation for costs related to exclusions and adjustments.

"The errors and inaccuracies in the reporting were specifically related to non-sporting and operational costs which the CCA recognised didn’t give the team any performance advantage, such as Marketing Activities, non-F1 Activities, HR Activities, Employee’s Bonus Costs, Offsetting of Costs, and Costs of Inventories.

"The team would also like to express its thanks to both the CCA and FIA, for its diligence and understanding throughout the entire process.

"The Financial Regulations are still relatively new, constantly evolving and complex, with some exclusions and adjustments being open to each team’s interpretation. The team acknowledges the collective efforts it needs to make across the business and recognises where improvements can be made in future."

The CAA, meanwhile, stated: "The Cost Cap Administration recognised that Alpine has acted cooperatively and in good faith throughout the review process and has sought to provide additional information and evidence when requested in a timely manner and that there is no accusation or evidence that Alpine has sought or obtained any undue advantage as a result of the Procedural Breach."
